about/this-site.html.title: THIS SITE
about/this-site.html.description:
Even this website is something interesting to talk about - at least to me.For the past 6 months or so I've been fairly enamored with using LLMs to build (mostly) software stuff. I've always enjoyed building things in the world of general internet-related technologies, and for the last half of my professional career I was either building, supporting, or monitoring enterprise tooling and platforms across several industries.I always enjoyed stumbling across a nice batteries-included tutorial to build some cool thing in docker, or some vendors detailed installation for their community-edition or self-hosted option.I, early-on, installed a proxmox server in my basement, and used portainer to make building platforms and docker-based applications super convenient.But now, using LLMs that are aware, by definition, of how everything is built and how they work, dynamic and mostly right tutorials are at our fingertips for ANYTHING - and simply by asking for it.
This site is constructed in Obsidian, and using an Obsidian plug-in written, coincidentally, by a fellow I know from the lab I am involved with at UofL, Nathan George, the Obsidian vault containing these pages can be exported as a complete website.Once the pages are exported locally, a typical static site publishing workflow is used to: make updates to a repo push that repo to github use github pages to 'publish' those pages to a publicly accessible URL
Here is that repo and here is an explanation / setup page I asked Claude to write for me when I was done.

projects/02-iths/curation/background.htm.title: background
projects/02-iths/curation/background.htm.description: started getting involved in the Curation committee of the 'Information Technology Historical Society' (https://iths.org).initial meeting today and had some very interesting topics to look into.they have a current database that was developed as part of a Drupal 7 website development.part of the discussion today was some history of that database, but also some new ideas and the possibilities for kind of starting over.i'd like to do some research on approaches, architectures, and tooling for what is basically: deciding on the structure of the ontology that supports the objectives of the organization graph and relational database technologies to implement such ontologies platform components to operate such technologies assuming the use of LLMs to assist in structuring queries to produce the desired user output here are a few of the functions of this ontology: records of IT hardware that have historical significance records of notable people within that industry a way to capture what ideas or innovations or products led to the next of same X and Y led to Z, or Z was inspired by X and Y canonical items for each but also user submissions of themselves (pictures or stories) with their copy or version of the canonical item timelines connecting items in interesting ways (inspiration tree or web, landmark items, etc.) i'd like some assistance in: how does a group determine what should be the structure of the ontology what is the process then to take that structured ontology and and develop the database to support it

projects/02-iths/curation/discussion-01..title: discussion-01
projects/02-iths/curation/discussion-01..description:
A working discussion space for figuring out how the ITHS Curation Committee should approach: Defining the structure of an ontology for IT historical artifacts, people, and relationships Translating that ontology into a database architecture Running the process collaboratively as a group (not just technically) An ontology for a historical society isn't just a schema. It's a set of claims about what kinds of things exist, how they relate, and what the organization believes is worth tracking. Before touching any database tool, the committee needs to answer questions like: What is the primary unit of record? (An artifact? A product line? A company? A person? An event?) What does "historical significance" mean for this organization? (Who decides? By what criteria?) How do we model influence and lineage? ("X led to Y" is a relationship, but there are many kinds of causality) What is the boundary between canonical record and user contribution? These are editorial and philosophical questions, not technical ones. The database follows from the answers.These examples are chosen because they faced the same core challenge: a community needed to agree on what things are before they could build anything.The Getty Research Institute maintains three controlled vocabularies — the Art & Architecture Thesaurus (AAT), the Union List of Artist Names (ULAN), and the Thesaurus of Geographic Names (TGN). These are among the most mature cultural heritage ontologies in existence.Relevance to ITHS: They separate concept records (what a thing is, abstractly) from instance records (a specific object or person) ULAN explicitly models relationships between artists: teacher/student, collaborator, influenced-by The AAT has a formal process for community submissions and editorial review — this maps well to the "canonical vs. user submission" problem Key lesson: They started with use cases, not with schema. "What questions do curators actually ask?" drove the structure.Reference: getty.edu/research/tools/vocabulariesWikidata is a general-purpose, community-maintained knowledge graph that underlies much of Wikipedia's structured data. Everything is a statement about an item, with properties and qualifiers.Relevance to ITHS: It explicitly handles the "X influenced Y" problem via properties like influenced by, has part, follows, followed by It has a clean separation between the item (canonical) and references (sourced claims) It's entirely open and the data model documentation is excellent for learning how to think about these problems Key lesson: Their data model evolved through community consensus via "WikiProjects" — groups that decided on the properties and structure for a domain (e.g., WikiProject Video Games, WikiProject Computing). This is a direct model for how the ITHS committee could work.
Reference: wikidata.org/wiki/Wikidata:WikiProjectsThe CHM has an online collection catalog that models hardware, software, people, and corporate history. They've had to solve the same "what is a canonical item?" question — is the canonical item the product design, the specific manufactured unit, or the product line?Relevance to ITHS: Their distinction between artifact (a physical thing), object type (a class of thing), and lot (a collection) maps onto the ITHS problem of personal submissions vs. canonical records They use a controlled vocabulary for significance/impact categories Key lesson: They distinguish "what the object is" from "what the object means" — physical description is separated from historical narrative. This prevents the ontology from collapsing under the weight of interpretation.
Reference: computerhistory.org/collections/Rick Prelinger's film archive and the broader Internet Archive have grappled with how to describe media items that have complex provenance chains — one film might be a copy of a copy, with annotations added by multiple hands.Relevance to ITHS: The "user submits their copy or story of a canonical item" feature is essentially a provenance and versioning problem Dublin Core and Schema.org (which IA uses heavily) are good prior art for simple, flat metadata that is still interoperable Key lesson: Don't invent what already exists. Dublin Core, Schema.org, and SKOS cover a huge amount of the basic metadata and relationship vocabulary. Start by mapping your concepts to these before creating custom properties.Open Library models the same three-tier structure that ITHS likely needs:Key lesson: This hierarchy is well-understood and worth adopting directly. It cleanly separates the abstract thing from its instantiations.
Reference: openlibrary.org/developers/apiBased on the above examples, here is a rough sequence for how the committee might work:Before any data modeling, collect 10–15 concrete questions that the database should be able to answer. Examples: "What hardware innovations came out of Xerox PARC and what products did they influence?" "Show me a timeline of storage media from punch cards to SSDs" "Who were the key engineers at DEC and what did they go on to build?" "What members have submitted photos of Apple I machines?" These become the test cases for the ontology. If a proposed schema can't answer them, it's incomplete.Working from the use cases, list the types of things and types of relationships that appear. Don't worry about the database yet. A whiteboard or a simple document is fine.Entity types might include: Person, Organization, Product, ProductLine, Concept/Innovation, Event, Document/Publication, PhysicalArtifact (user submission).Relationship types might include: EmployedBy, InventedBy, InfluencedBy, PrecededBy, PartOf, VersionOf, ContributedTo.Before designing custom schema, check if Schema.org, Wikidata properties, or the Getty AAT already have the concept. This saves time and enables future interoperability.Write entity definitions and relationship definitions in plain sentences before touching any technical notation. Example: A Product is a commercially released item (hardware or software) with a known manufacturer and release date. A Product may have a PrecededBy relationship to another Product if the earlier Product was a direct technical or commercial predecessor. Pick one domain (e.g., personal computers from 1975–1985) and build the schema for just that slice. Load a small amount of real data. See what breaks.Only after Phases 1–5 is it worth deciding: relational, graph, or hybrid? Document store? The answer should fall out of the data naturally, not be chosen up front. What is the minimum viable set of entity types to launch with? Who has editorial authority over canonical records vs. user submissions? Is the goal a public-facing database, an internal curatorial tool, or both? What existing databases (Wikidata, CHM catalog) should we link to rather than duplicate? How do we handle contested history? (Competing claims of "who invented X") Share this doc with the committee for feedback Schedule a use-case collection session (Phase 1) Identify which committee members have worked with any of the reference systems above Look at the existing Drupal 7 database schema — what entities does it already have?

projects/02-iths/general/this-is-it.html.title: this is IT
projects/02-iths/general/this-is-it.html.description:
Approaches and suggestions for defining Information TechnologyRestricting IT to computers is a common but historically shallow framing. It ignores the decades of foundational work that made computing possible — and the broader truth that information, not hardware, is the subject. The better question is: what does IT do? It captures, processes, stores, transmits, and retrieves information. The machinery changes; the mission doesn't.Define IT by what it does, not what it is made of:
Any technology whose primary purpose is to handle information — acquiring, storing, processing, transmitting, or displaying it.
This immediately includes:
Telegraphs and telephone switches
Radio and television broadcasting infrastructure
Punch card systems (pre-electronic)
Modern computing, networking, and AI
Why this works: It's technology-agnostic and future-proof. When something new arrives (quantum computing, biological computing), you can ask "does it handle information?" rather than "does it look like a computer?"Trace IT back to its intellectual origins rather than its commercial ones.Key waypoints:
1840s — Telegraph: the first system to separate information from a physical carrier (the message from the messenger)
1876 — Telephone: real-time voice as data
Bell Labs (1920s–1970s) — Transistor, information theory, Shannon's entropy, error correction, signal processing. This is arguably the true birthplace of modern IT
1948 — Claude Shannon's A Mathematical Theory of Communication — the foundational paper that defines information mathematically and underpins all digital systems
1950s–60s — Mainframe computing emerges from this lineage, not apart from it
1970s–present — Personal computing, internet, mobile, cloud
The takeaway: computers didn't create IT; IT created computers. The field existed before the transistor.Information technology is a subset of the broader field of information science, which includes:
How information is structured and classified (library science, ontologies, metadata)
How it is communicated (linguistics, semiotics, media studies)
How it is secured and controlled (cryptography, policy)
How it is used by humans (HCI, cognitive science)
This approach connects IT to disciplines that don't typically appear in a CS curriculum but are inseparable from it in practice. Cybersecurity, UX, data governance, and AI ethics all live here.IT doesn't exist in isolation — it's always embedded in social systems. Defining it purely as hardware or software misses the human layer.
IT is the ensemble of tools, practices, standards, and institutions that societies use to manage information.
This includes:
Postal systems (organised information routing)
Filing and records management
Standards bodies (IEEE, IETF, ISO) — the "invisible infrastructure"
Data centres as physical/social infrastructure
Why this is useful for teaching: It prevents students from thinking of IT as purely technical, which helps when addressing ethics, policy, and real-world impact.For a more rigorous framing: information, in the technical sense, is reduction of uncertainty. IT is any system that does this systematically.A traffic light is a rudimentary IT system. A spreadsheet is an IT system. So is a filing cabinet. What makes modern IT distinctive is:
Scale (billions of operations, billions of users)
Speed (real-time or near-real-time)
Programmability (the system can be reconfigured without physical change)
This framing lets you distinguish IT from other technologies while explaining why electronics and software became central — they maximise all three properties.Rather than one rigid definition, consider a layered scope:The "core" is what most people mean by IT in everyday use. The outer layers are what separate a practitioner from a technician. Open with Bell Labs — it's one of the most productive research environments in history and draws a direct line from physics → information theory → computing → the internet. It immediately challenges the "IT = computers" assumption. Use Shannon's definition of information as an early anchor. It's rigorous, non-circular, and gives students a durable mental model that survives technological change. Include one non-digital case study (e.g., the London postal system in the 1800s, or telephone exchange operators) to demonstrate that information systems predate electronics. Frame computers as an instantiation of IT, not its definition — the way an internal combustion engine is one instantiation of the idea of a heat engine. Acknowledge the fuzzy boundary — IT overlaps with electrical engineering, communications, media, and management. That's not a weakness; it's evidence that information is genuinely central to modern life. Document created: 2026-02-26

projects/03-bible-study/episode-03/01-ep.description:
The Gospel of John with Dr. John Bergsma
Scripture Focus: John 3–5In this episode, Dr. Bergsma discusses John 3–5, focusing on the image of Our Lord as Divine Bridegroom of Israel. He begins by examining the figures of Nicodemus and John the Baptist, who both appear in John 3. Through Our Lord's conversation with Nicodemus, it becomes clear that, out of love for us, Jesus came to free us from sin and darkness. This is a powerful truth intimately connected with our baptism. Dr. Bergsma walks through Jesus' encounter with the Samaritan woman, who, despite appearances, longs for the coming Messiah. Finally, Dr. Bergsma concludes this episode by discussing two of the "signs" performed by Our Lord: the healing of the official's son, and the healing of the paralytic.
Nicodemus asks Jesus about being "born again", foreshadowing baptism
John the Baptist identifies Jesus as the Bridegroom
Jesus meets the Samaritan woman at Jacob's well. He reveals Himself as the Messiah & Bridegroom of Israel
Healing the official's son: Anointing of the Sick
Healing the paralytic: Sacrament of Reconciliation

projects/03-bible-study/episode-03/02-re.title: 02- review
projects/03-bible-study/episode-03/02-re.description:
Jesus Christ, Divine Bridegroom
Scripture Focus: John 3–5In John 3:1-2, Nicodemus comes to Jesus by night. What does this action symbolize?
a. A lack of knowledge
b. The light of the Holy Spirit
c. Spiritual darkness
d. Both A & C
To understand why Nicodemus coming "by night" carries such weight, we must first appreciate the literary and theological architecture of John's Gospel. From the very opening of the Prologue, St. John establishes a governing cosmic opposition: light and darkness.
"The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it." (John 1:5)
This is not merely poetic atmosphere. For John, light and darkness are moral and spiritual categories. Light is identified with Christ Himself — "I am the light of the world" (John 8:12) — and with the illuminating grace of the Holy Spirit. Darkness, by contrast, is the condition of the soul that has not yet received that illumination. It is the natural habitat of sin, ignorance, and unbelief.When John tells us that Nicodemus came to Jesus by night, he is doing something the Church Fathers recognized immediately: he is placing Nicodemus squarely within the realm of darkness — not as a moral condemnation, but as a theological statement about his current spiritual condition.Darkness as Spiritual Blindness (option C)Nicodemus is a Pharisee and "a ruler of the Jews" — a man of considerable religious standing. He even acknowledges that Jesus comes from God ("no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him", John 3:2). And yet, for all his religious learning, he remains in the dark. He has not yet come to faith. He approaches Jesus secretly, under cover of night, because the full light of revelation has not yet pierced his heart.St. Augustine, commenting on this passage, notes that Nicodemus represents those souls who possess a kind of preliminary faith — they see the signs, they sense the divine presence — but have not yet made the full passage from darkness to light. He writes that Nicodemus "came to Jesus, but came by night; that is, he came to the Light, but came in darkness." The darkness is not merely external. It is the condition of his interior life at that moment.Darkness as Lack of Understanding (option A)This same darkness is expressed immediately in what follows. When Jesus tells Nicodemus that "unless one is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God" (John 3:3), Nicodemus responds with a question that reveals how deeply carnal — how earthbound — his thinking still is: "How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother's womb and be born?" (John 3:4).He hears the words of eternal life and interprets them biologically. He stands before the Word made flesh and cannot yet read the language of the Spirit. This is precisely the lack of knowledge that the darkness symbolizes. His mind is not yet illumined by grace, and so the spiritual realities Jesus speaks of remain opaque to him.St. Cyril of Alexandria draws the same connection: Nicodemus's inability to understand spiritual rebirth flows from the very darkness he carries into the encounter. Knowledge and light, in Johannine theology, are inseparable. To be in darkness is to be without true understanding.Why not option B?Option B — "the light of the Holy Spirit" — is precisely the opposite of what the night represents. The Holy Spirit is the agent of illumination, the one who leads us into all truth (John 16:13). To come by night is to come before that illumination has taken hold. It is the absence of the Holy Spirit's light, not its presence.The Catechism and Baptismal TypologyIt is worth noting that the Church has always read this passage in close connection with the Sacrament of Baptism. The Catechism of the Catholic Church teaches that Baptism is the sacrament of illumination (CCC 1216), drawing directly on the early Christian title for Baptism: photismos — enlightenment. To be baptized is to pass from darkness into the marvelous light of Christ (1 Peter 2:9).Nicodemus's night visit, then, is not merely a narrative detail. It is a theological portrait of the soul before Baptism — dwelling in spiritual darkness and ignorance, yet drawn nonetheless toward the Light. Jesus does not send him away. He meets him in the darkness and speaks to him of water and the Spirit (John 3:5). The very conversation foreshadows what Baptism will accomplish: the passage from night into light, from ignorance into knowledge, from death into new life.True or False: The Samaritan woman's adultery is symbolic of the idolatrous history of the Northern tribes.At first reading, the encounter at Jacob's Well in John 4 appears to be a straightforward story of personal conversion: a woman with a troubled past meets Jesus, comes to recognize Him as the Messiah, and runs to tell her village. And it is certainly that. But the Catholic tradition, following the method of the Church Fathers and rooted in the deep logic of salvation history, recognizes that John has embedded a far richer meaning in the detail that the woman has had five husbands — and that the man she currently lives with is not her husband.The Historical Key: 2 Kings 17To grasp the symbolism, we must go back to one of the most consequential events in Israel's history: the fall of the Northern Kingdom of Samaria to the Assyrian Empire in 722 BC. The Assyrian policy was to displace conquered populations. When they deported the Israelites of the North, they repopulated the land with five foreign nations:
"And the king of Assyria brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim, and placed them in the cities of Samaria instead of the people of Israel." (2 Kings 17:24)
Each of these five nations brought its own gods. The text goes on to describe the syncretistic religion that resulted — a mixture of the worship of Yahweh with the worship of the gods of these foreign peoples (2 Kings 17:29-41). The Samaritans thus became a people who, as the text says, "feared the Lord but also served their own gods."Five nations. Five foreign gods. Five husbands.The Prophetic Background: Israel as Unfaithful BrideThis identification is not an interpretive novelty. The entire prophetic tradition of the Old Testament consistently employs the marriage metaphor to describe the covenant between God and Israel — and Israel's idolatry as adultery against the divine Bridegroom.The prophet Hosea is commanded by God to marry a faithless woman as a living parable of this reality (Hosea 1–3). Ezekiel gives an even more extended and devastating account of Israel's spiritual adultery in chapters 16 and 23, describing how Jerusalem and Samaria played the harlot with the nations around them. Jeremiah uses the same language (Jeremiah 3). In every case, the idolatry of the Northern tribes — their abandonment of the one true God for the gods of the nations — is spoken of as marital unfaithfulness.When Jesus speaks to the Samaritan woman and reveals that she has had five husbands, He is not merely exposing her personal sin. He is speaking the language of the prophets to the daughter of the Northern Kingdom. You have had five husbands — five false gods, five nations, five objects of your misplaced worship. And the one you have now is not your husband — the current spiritual disorder, the ongoing syncretic half-worship that has marked Samaria for centuries, is no true covenant at all.Jesus as the True Bridegroom of IsraelThis is why the scene takes place at Jacob's Well. In the Old Testament, wells are betrothal sites. Abraham's servant finds a wife for Isaac at a well. Jacob meets Rachel at a well. Moses meets Zipporah at a well. The pattern is unmistakable: a man meets a woman at a well, and a marriage covenant follows. John's first readers would have recognized this pattern immediately.Jesus comes to Jacob's Well not as a passing traveler but as the Divine Bridegroom of Israel, come to reclaim His unfaithful Bride. He offers her not ordinary water but living water — a spousal gift, the gift of Himself, the gift of the Holy Spirit (John 7:37-39). He reveals that He knows her history — all five husbands — not to shame her, but to show her that He knows her fully and loves her still.This is the deepest logic of the Incarnation itself, as the Catechism teaches: "The entire Christian life bears the mark of the spousal love of Christ and the Church" (CCC 1617). The New Covenant is a New Marriage. And Jesus comes to Samaria — to the very heartland of Israel's ancient faithlessness — to offer that covenant to a woman who embodies the whole history of her people's wandering.The Samaritan Woman as Icon of the ChurchThe Church Fathers, particularly Origen and St. Augustine, read the Samaritan woman as a type of the Church drawn from the Gentile nations — longing, without knowing it, for the true Bridegroom. Her words "I know that Messiah is coming" (John 4:25) reveal a deeper hunger beneath all her restless searching. She has been seeking the wrong husbands all along. In Christ, she finds the One for whom her heart was made.This is the Catholic reading of Scripture at its most beautiful: nothing is wasted, nothing is merely incidental. The five husbands of one woman at a well in Samaria carry the weight of centuries of salvation history — and point forward to the mercy of the Divine Bridegroom who came to make all things new.

projects/03-bible-study/episode-03/03-re.title: 03 - reflection
projects/03-bible-study/episode-03/03-re.description:
Jesus Christ, Divine Bridegroom
Scripture Focus: John 3–5Every year on the Third Sunday in Lent, the Church invites the faithful to reflect on the story of the woman at the well. In light of what Dr. Bergsma shared in this episode, why do you think the Church returns to this passage year after year? What aspects of the Samaritan woman's story reflect the themes of the Lenten season?The Church is never arbitrary in her liturgical choices. When she returns to a text year after year — and she has done so for centuries — it is because she has discerned in that text an inexhaustible depth of spiritual nourishment suited to a particular moment in the sacred year. The story of the Samaritan woman at Jacob's Well (John 4:1–42) is one of the most theologically dense passages in all of Sacred Scripture, and its placement on the Third Sunday of Lent is an act of profound pastoral wisdom.The Lenten Context: Preparation for BaptismTo understand why the Church chooses this passage for Lent, we must first recall what Lent actually is. It is not, at its origins, merely a season of personal penance for the already baptized. Its ancient heart is catechumenal — it is the final and most intense stage of preparation for those who will receive Baptism at the Easter Vigil. The Third, Fourth, and Fifth Sundays of Lent in Year A of the lectionary correspond to the three great scrutinies — solemn rites of purification and enlightenment celebrated with the elect, those preparing to enter the Church.The scrutinies are precisely what the name suggests: an honest examination, before God and the community, of the condition of the soul. They are a laying bare of interior darkness so that it might be driven out and replaced with the light of Christ. And there is no better icon of this movement in all of Scripture than the Samaritan woman.She comes to the well alone, at noon — the sixth hour, when the sun is highest and shadows are shortest. Some commentators have seen in this detail the opposite of Nicodemus: she comes in full light, but her life is one of hidden darkness. She has been drawing water alone, likely because the shame of her history has made her an outcast from the company of the other women who would come at dawn. She is isolated by sin, just as every soul preparing for Baptism must come to recognize their isolation from God through the weight of sin.The Dynamics of ConversionWhat unfolds at the well is a masterclass in the dynamics of conversion — which is why the Church, in her wisdom, returns to it every year. Jesus does not begin with accusation. He begins with thirst: "Give me a drink" (John 4:7). He enters the woman's world, meets her where she is, and draws her into conversation. This is the pattern of divine grace: it does not overwhelm but invites, not condemns but reveals.As the conversation deepens, Jesus gently brings her to the point of self-knowledge. "Go, call your husband" (John 4:16). He already knows the answer. He is not gathering information — He is inviting her to honesty, to the same interior examination that the scrutinies demand of the elect. And she responds, to her credit, with a kind of courageous half-truth: "I have no husband." Jesus honors the truth in her words and fills in what she left unspoken.This movement — from evasion to acknowledgment, from the surface to the depths — is the essential movement of Lent. It is the movement of metanoia, the Greek word the Church uses for repentance, meaning not merely feeling sorry but a turning of the mind, a reorientation of the whole person toward God.Thirst as the Lenten ConditionAt the deepest level, the story of the Samaritan woman is a story about thirst. She comes to the well because she is physically thirsty. But Jesus diagnoses a deeper thirst beneath the surface — the thirst of a soul that has been seeking in all the wrong places the one thing that can satisfy: living communion with the living God."Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again, but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again." (John 4:13–14)This is one of the most penetrating lines in the Gospel. It is a description of every human life lived without God. We keep returning to the same wells — pleasure, approval, comfort, distraction — and they keep running dry. The woman has had five husbands. She has tried again and again to fill the aching void at the center of her life. And Jesus meets her in that exhaustion with an offer that changes everything.Lent is the season when the Church asks us to sit with our thirst. To stop filling ourselves with things that do not satisfy and allow ourselves to feel, honestly, how deep the longing goes. The Samaritan woman is our companion in this. Her transformation — from isolated, shame-ridden outcast to the first evangelist of her village — is the promise of what Lent, lived well, can accomplish in each of us.Baptismal TypologyFinally, we cannot miss the sacramental dimension. The Catechism of the Catholic Church identifies water, from the very first pages of Genesis, as a primary symbol of the Holy Spirit's action (CCC 694). The living water Jesus offers the Samaritan woman is, as He Himself will make explicit in John 7:38–39, the Holy Spirit. And the Holy Spirit is given preeminently in Baptism.The Church places this passage before her catechumens in the final weeks before their Baptism because it is a portrait of what is about to happen to them. They, like the woman, are about to receive living water. They, like her, will be known completely by the One who gives it — and loved completely in that knowledge. And they, like her, will be sent to proclaim what they have received.What are your thoughts on the connection between the "living water" Jesus offers the Samaritan woman and the description of Solomon's bride as a "well of living water" in Song of Songs 4:15?The connection between John 4 and Song of Songs 4:15 is one of the most beautiful instances of typological fulfillment in all of Scripture, and it has not been lost on the great tradition of Catholic biblical interpretation.The Text of Song of SongsIn Song of Songs 4:15, the bridegroom Solomon addresses his bride with an extraordinary image:
"A garden fountain, a well of living water, and flowing streams from Lebanon."
The bride herself is described as a source of living water. She is the well from which the bridegroom draws life and refreshment. The entire section (4:12–5:1) describes the bride as a locked garden, a sealed fountain — an image of purity, abundance, and the intimate exclusivity of the covenant bond. She is, for her bridegroom, the source of everything he needs.The Church, following the great Origen in his Commentary on the Song of Songs, has always read this text on multiple levels simultaneously. At the literal level, it is a love poem celebrating human marriage. But at the deeper allegorical level — and the Fathers are unanimous that this deeper reading is the text's primary spiritual meaning — the bridegroom is God, and the bride is Israel and, by extension, the Church and the individual soul.The Inversion and Its MeaningNow consider what happens in John 4. Jesus, the Divine Bridegroom, comes to the Samaritan woman — a daughter of the lost Northern Kingdom, a figure of Israel's scattered and wayward Bride — at a well. And He does not draw water from her. Instead, He offers her living water from Himself.Here is the profound inversion that the typology makes visible: in Song of Songs, the bride is the well of living water for the bridegroom. In John 4, the Bridegroom offers living water to a bride who has run completely dry.This is not a contradiction but a fulfillment. It shows us the precise nature of what sin has done to Israel — and to every human soul. The bride who was meant, in God's original design, to be a garden fountain, a well of living water, has become instead a woman returning daily to an earthly well, drawing water that cannot satisfy. The image of the Song has been shattered by the history of human faithlessness.And so the Divine Bridegroom comes — not to condemn the broken image, but to restore it. He offers her the living water that will become in her "a spring of water welling up to eternal life" (John 4:14). He is not taking from her. He is giving her back what she was always meant to be.The Holy Spirit as Living WaterJesus identifies this living water explicitly with the Holy Spirit in John 7:38–39:
"Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, 'Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water.' Now this he said about the Spirit."
The Holy Spirit is the living water of the New Covenant. And the reception of the Holy Spirit — particularly in Baptism and Confirmation — restores to the soul what sin had taken away: the capacity to be, in the language of Song of Songs, a garden fountain, a source of living water for others.This is what the Samaritan woman becomes. She receives the living water from Jesus. She returns to her village. And from her flows the evangelistic proclamation that brings her whole community to Christ. She is transformed, by encounter with the Bridegroom, from a dry and isolated woman into the very thing Solomon celebrated in his bride: a well of living water for those around her.The Cross as the Deepest FulfillmentWe cannot close this reflection without noting that the ultimate source of this living water is the pierced side of Christ on Calvary. John tells us with deliberate solemnity: "one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once blood and water came out" (John 19:34). The Church Fathers — Augustine most memorably — saw in this the birth of the Church from the side of the New Adam, just as Eve was drawn from the side of the first Adam. The living water that flows from Christ's wounded side is the water of Baptism, and the blood is the Eucharist.The Bridegroom gives Himself entirely for His Bride. He becomes, on the Cross, the inexhaustible well of living water that His Bride was always meant to be.Dr. Bergsma described the man Jesus healed in John 5 as an "icon of the people of Israel." When you examine this passage, what dimensions of the paralyzed man's story reflect the history of the Israelites in the Old Testament? What aspects of the man's encounter with Our Lord can offer insight into the Christian life today?The healing of the paralytic at the Pool of Bethesda (John 5:1–15) is, on the surface, a straightforward miracle story. But once we read it with the eyes of the tradition — trained to see how the New Testament is the Old Testament unveiled — it becomes something far more: a compressed retelling of Israel's entire salvation history, and a mirror held up to the condition of every human soul in need of God's healing grace.The Number 38: An Unmistakable SignalJohn tells us that the man had been lying by the pool for thirty-eight years. This number is not chosen at random. For a reader steeped in the Old Testament, it would have resonated immediately with one of the most painful passages in the Pentateuch.In Deuteronomy 2:14, Moses recalls the years of Israel's wandering and notes:
"And the time from our leaving Kadesh-barnea until we crossed the brook Zered was thirty-eight years, until the entire generation, the men of war, had perished from the camp, as the Lord had sworn to them."
Thirty-eight years: the precise duration of Israel's punishment in the desert, the period during which the faithless generation that refused to enter the Promised Land was consigned to paralysis, to going nowhere, to waiting for death while the next generation grew up. The paralytic has been lying by the pool for exactly this length of time. John is waving a flag for his theologically literate readers: this man is Israel.The Pool and the LawThe Pool of Bethesda had five porticoes — and lying under those five porticoes were the multitudes of the sick, the blind, the lame, and the paralyzed, waiting for the water to be stirred. The Church Fathers, including Tertullian and later commentators, noted that five porticoes correspond to the five books of Moses — the Torah. Under the canopy of the Law, Israel lay sick and waiting.This is a precise theological statement about the limits of the Mosaic Law. The Law, as St. Paul will later articulate with such force in his letters to the Romans and Galatians, was never designed to justify — to save — but to diagnose. It revealed the condition of sin but could not heal it. The paralytic lies under five porticoes, waiting. The Law surrounds him. But the Law cannot make him rise.Helplessness and the Need for a SaviorThe most piercing moment of this story is the paralytic's answer to Jesus's question: "Do you want to be healed?" (John 5:6). We might expect a simple yes. Instead, we get a lament:
"Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred up, and while I am going another steps down before me." (John 5:7)
He has no one. Thirty-eight years, and no one has helped him. He is utterly dependent on others and utterly abandoned by them. This is Israel in Egypt — enslaved, powerless, unable to save themselves, with no deliverer in sight. It is Israel in the desert — unable to enter the land, incapable of claiming what God had promised. And in a deeper sense, it is every human soul in the condition of sin: paralyzed, unable to rise by its own power, perpetually displaced by those more agile or more favored, waiting for a healing that never comes.This helplessness is not incidental. It is the very condition that makes the miracle possible — and that makes its meaning legible. Jesus does not come to those who have managed to limp to the pool on their own. He comes to the one who has been lying there the longest, who has the least hope, who has no one."Rise, Take Up Your Mat, and Walk"Jesus does not ask for effort or merit. He commands. "Rise, take up your bed, and walk" (John 5:8). Three imperatives. And the man rises.This is the new Exodus. Moses stretched out his staff; the sea parted. Jesus speaks, and a man paralyzed for thirty-eight years stands upright and walks. He is, in his person, the crossing of the Jordan — the end of the long paralysis, the entry into the land that could not be achieved under the Law. What the five porticoes could not accomplish, a single word from the Son of God accomplishes instantly.The Catechism, in its treatment of the Sacrament of Penance, notes that the healings of Jesus in the Gospels are signs of the forgiveness and restoration that He confers through the sacraments of the Church (CCC 1503–1504). The study guide itself draws the explicit connection: the healing of the paralytic points to the Sacrament of Reconciliation. This is not an imposition but a recognition. Jesus's final word to the man — "Sin no more, that nothing worse may happen to you" (John 5:14) — makes the connection between the physical healing and the interior healing of the soul undeniable.The Man's Response: A WarningWe cannot idealize the paralytic's response. When the Jewish authorities confront him about carrying his mat on the Sabbath, he deflects responsibility: "The man who healed me told me to" (John 5:11). And then, upon learning that his healer is Jesus, he goes and reports this to those who are seeking to persecute Him (John 5:15).This, too, mirrors Israel's history — the pattern of receiving grace and failing to respond with corresponding gratitude and fidelity. The healed man does not seek out his healer to give thanks. He does not follow Him. He does not become a disciple. And in this he stands as a warning to all of us who receive the grace of the sacraments and then drift back into old habits, old paralysis, old indifference.Application for the Christian LifeThe man's story is our story. There are areas of every Christian life that have been paralyzed for years — perhaps decades. Sins we have confessed and returned to. Wounds we have carried so long we have come to regard them as permanent. Interior attitudes that have kept us lying by the same pool, watching others receive what we cannot seem to reach.Jesus asks us the same question He asked the paralytic: "Do you want to be healed?" It is a more searching question than it appears. Sometimes our paralysis has become our identity. We are not sure who we would be without it. The healing Jesus offers requires that we rise — that we actually pick up our mat and walk, leaving behind the place where we have been lying for so long.The Sacrament of Reconciliation is the privileged place where this encounter happens. The priest, acting in persona Christi, speaks the words of absolution — and Christ speaks through them as surely as He spoke to the paralytic by the pool. The thirty-eight years of waiting can end in a single moment of grace.But the grace demands a response. "Sin no more." To receive the healing of Reconciliation and return to the same sin is to act as the paralytic did — to take the gift and walk away from the Giver. The Christian life is not a series of returns to the pool but a sustained walking: the daily choosing, in cooperation with grace, to remain upright, to remain free, to remain in the company of the One who first commanded us to rise.

projects/03-bible-study/episode-03/04-pr.title: 04 - practical-application
projects/03-bible-study/episode-03/04-pr.description:
Jesus Christ, Divine Bridegroom
Scripture Focus: John 4:1–42This week, try doing lectio divina prayer with the story of the Samaritan woman (John 4:1–41). Ask the Holy Spirit to help you listen to God's voice. Read slowly through the passage as many times as you need. When you encounter a word or phrase that stands out to you, pause and meditate on it. Enter into loving conversation with the Lord. Talk to Him openly and honestly about what you notice coming up in your heart as you reflect on this story.Lectio divina — Latin for "sacred reading" — is one of the oldest and most venerable forms of prayer in the Catholic tradition. Rooted in the practice of the Desert Fathers and systematized by St. Benedict in the sixth century, it was described by the twelfth-century monk Guigo II as a ladder of four rungs by which the soul ascends toward God:1. Lectio — Reading
Read the passage slowly and attentively, as though hearing it for the first time. This is not study — it is listening. Read aloud if possible. Let the words land. When a word, phrase, or image arrests your attention, stop. You do not need to finish the passage. The Holy Spirit has something to say to you there.2. Meditatio — Meditation
Remain with the word or phrase that caught your attention. Repeat it gently, turn it over in your mind, allow it to descend from the head into the heart. Ask: Why does this word stand out to me? What is God showing me through it? What does it reveal about His heart — or mine?3. Oratio — Prayer
Respond to God from the heart. This is conversation, not performance. Tell Him honestly what you are feeling — confusion, longing, gratitude, resistance, joy. The Samaritan woman spoke to Jesus plainly and imperfectly, and He received every word. So will He receive yours.4. Contemplatio — Contemplation
Rest. Allow yourself to simply be in God's presence without words or effort. This is the gift that the other three movements prepare us for — a quiet, loving awareness of the One who is already present.Note: Do not feel pressure to move through all four stages in a single sitting. Sometimes the Spirit holds you at Lectio for the entire time. This is not failure — it is fidelity to where God is working.Come, Holy Spirit, fill the hearts of your faithful,
and kindle in them the fire of your love.
Send forth your Spirit and they shall be created,
and you shall renew the face of the earth.O God, who by the light of the Holy Spirit
did instruct the hearts of the faithful,
grant that by the same Holy Spirit
we may be truly wise and ever enjoy His consolations.
Through Christ our Lord. Amen.New American Bible, Revised Edition (NABRE)1 Now when Jesus learned that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John 2 (although Jesus himself was not baptizing, just his disciples), 3 he left Judea and returned to Galilee.The Samaritan Woman4 He had to pass through Samaria. 5 So he came to a town of Samaria called Sychar, near the plot of land that Jacob had given to his son Joseph. 6 Jacob's well was there. Jesus, tired from his journey, sat down there at the well. It was about noon.7 A woman of Samaria came to draw water. Jesus said to her, "Give me a drink." 8 His disciples had gone into the town to buy food. 9 The Samaritan woman said to him, "How can you, a Jew, ask me, a Samaritan woman, for a drink?" (For Jews use nothing in common with Samaritans.) 10 Jesus answered and said to her, "If you knew the gift of God and who is saying to you, 'Give me a drink,' you would have asked him and he would have given you living water."11 The woman said to him, "Sir, you do not even have a bucket and the well is deep; where then can you get this living water? 12 Are you greater than our father Jacob, who gave us this well and drank from it himself with his children and his flocks?" 13 Jesus answered and said to her, "Everyone who drinks this water will be thirsty again; 14 but whoever drinks the water I shall give will never thirst; the water I shall give will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life." 15 The woman said to him, "Sir, give me this water, so that I may not be thirsty or have to keep coming here to draw water."16 Jesus said to her, "Go call your husband and come back." 17 The woman answered and said to him, "I do not have a husband." Jesus answered her, "You are right in saying, 'I do not have a husband.' 18 For you have had five husbands, and the one you have now is not your husband. What you have said is true." 19 The woman said to him, "Sir, I can see that you are a prophet. 20 Our ancestors worshiped on this mountain; but you people say that the place to worship is in Jerusalem."21 Jesus said to her, "Believe me, woman, the hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem. 22 You people worship what you do not understand; we worship what we understand, because salvation is from the Jews. 23 But the hour is coming, and is now here, when true worshipers will worship the Father in Spirit and truth; and indeed the Father seeks such people to worship him. 24 God is Spirit, and those who worship him must worship in Spirit and truth." 25 The woman said to him, "I know that the Messiah is coming, the one called the Anointed; when he comes, he will tell us everything." 26 Jesus said to her, "I am he, the one who is speaking with you."27 At that moment his disciples returned, and were amazed that he was talking with a woman, but still no one said, "What are you looking for?" or "Why are you talking with her?" 28 The woman left her water jar and went into the town and said to the people, 29 "Come see a man who told me everything I have done. Could he possibly be the Messiah?" 30 They went out of the town and came to him.31 Meanwhile, the disciples urged him, "Rabbi, eat." 32 But he said to them, "I have food to eat of which you do not know." 33 So the disciples said to one another, "Could someone have brought him something to eat?" 34 Jesus said to them, "My food is to do the will of the one who sent me and to finish his work. 35 Do you not say, 'In four months the harvest will be here'? I tell you, look up and see the fields ripe for the harvest. 36 The reaper is already receiving his payment and gathering crops for eternal life, so that the sower and reaper can rejoice together. 37 For here the saying is verified that 'One sows and another reaps.' 38 I sent you to reap what you have not worked for; others have done the work, and you are sharing the fruits of their work."39 Many of the Samaritans of that town began to believe in him because of the word of the woman who testified, "He told me everything I have done." 40 When the Samaritans came to him, they invited him to stay with them; and he stayed there two days. 41 Many more began to believe in him because of his word, 42 and they said to the woman, "We no longer believe because of your word; for we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this is truly the savior of the world."The word or phrase that stood out to me:What I noticed in my heart as I sat with it:What I said to the Lord (Oratio):What I received in the quiet (Contemplatio):
